food.text: The Lapita people began settling Island Melanesia through seaborne migration around 1600 BCE. They kept pigs, dogs, and chickens as domesticated farm animals.
The Lapita people grew root crops and tree crops such as taro, yam, coconuts, bananas, and varieties of breadfruit. These plants formed the basis of their horticulture across Island Melanesia.
Austronesian peoples carried taro into the Pacific Islands from around 1300 BC. There it became a staple crop of Polynesian communities.

Austronesians colonized the Northern Mariana Islands by 1500 BCE, becoming the first humans to reach Remote Oceania. This Chamorro migration was the only Austronesian migration into the Pacific Islands to successfully retain rice cultivation.

The Lapita produced their classic pottery in the Bismarck Archipelago between 1600 and 1200 BCE. Their villages tended to be located on the beach or on small offshore islets, with some houses built on stilts over lagoons.

These domesticated coconuts became a critical resource for Austronesian voyagers on long sea voyages. They provided a portable source of food and water, as well as building materials for Austronesian outrigger boats.

food.text: Breadfruit spread into Oceania via the Austronesian expansion. In Polynesia it is believed to have been selectively bred from the wild breadnut, Artocarpus camansi.
Alongside their famous pottery decorated with dentate stamps, the Lapita later also produced plainer, undecorated pottery, found across many Western Polynesian islands.

Austronesian peoples began spreading from Southeast Asia into the edges of Micronesia and Melanesia from around 3000 BC. Polynesian double-hulled canoes had two equal-length hulls lashed side by side, with space between them used to store food, hunting materials, and nets on long voyages.
The Chamorro migration to the Mariana Islands was unique among Austronesian migrations to the Pacific Islands. It was the only one to successfully retain rice cultivation.

art.text: The oldest known pottery in Oceania comes from the Marianas Islands. It is decorated with circle- and punctate/dentate-stamped patterns and is securely dated to 1500 BCE–1300 BCE from multiple archaeological sites.

In the mid-2nd millennium BC, a distinctive culture called Lapita appeared in the Bismarck Archipelago. It is especially known for pottery, including many vessels of varied shapes, some distinguished by fine patterns and motifs pressed into the clay.

Around 1500 BC, art began to appear in New Guinea, including the earliest examples of sculpture in Oceania. This sculpture appears as stone figures found throughout the island, mostly in the mountainous highlands, and one has been dated to 1500 BC. The freestanding figures portray humans, animals, and phalluses, and the tops of many pestles carry images of birds or human heads. Their original significance is unknown, but they were perhaps used in rituals.
Lapita potters decorated their ware with dentate-stamped geometric designs. Classic Lapita pottery was produced between 1,600 and 1,200 BCE on the Bismarck Archipelago.
The Marianas pottery of 1500 BCE–1300 BCE is older than the earliest Lapita culture pottery, which dates to about 1350–1300 BCE. This makes it the earliest known pottery in Oceania.

The Marianas pottery most closely resembles a subset of Nagsabaran pottery from the northern Philippines. Hung et al. (2011) proposed a direct voyage from eastern Luzon, which would have been the longest sea crossing in human history up to that time, though this remains disputed.

science.text: Austronesian seafarers used sails some time before 2000 BCE. Combined with catamarans, outrigger boats, lashed-lug boats and the crab claw sail, this technology let them spread rapidly across the islands of the Indo-Pacific.
Anthropologists and historians believe the Great Polynesian Migration began around 1500 BC. Austronesian peoples used celestial navigation to find islands in the South Pacific Ocean.
Outrigger boats were the first true ocean-going ships. They carried the Austronesian expansion from Taiwan into the islands of the Indian and Pacific Oceans from around 3000 BC.

The coconut was domesticated by Austronesian peoples and spread across the Pacific on their seaborne migrations. It was vital on long voyages, giving them portable food and water as well as building materials for outrigger boats.

science.text: An outrigger or double-hull vessel gets its stability from the distance between its hulls, not from the shape of each hull. This is why such hulls can be longer, narrower and more hydrodynamically efficient than those of single-hull vessels.
Polynesian double-hulled canoes were two large hulls of equal length, lashed side by side. The space between them could hold food, hunting materials and nets for long voyages.

The 2022 genetic study found Papuan ancestry among the peoples of Central Micronesia and Palau, but not among those of the Mariana Islands. It also supports the Admiralty Islands as the source of the Central Micronesian peoples and languages.

Outriggers may have first been needed for stability on small boats after the invention of crab claw sails around 1500 BCE. Pacific sailors later handled the problem of tacking with a shunting technique and reversible single outriggers.

The Lapita complex appears suddenly on the Bismarck Archipelago around 3,500 years ago, already fully developed. No earlier stages have been found there, which suggests the technology was brought by migrants rather than invented locally.

Only Pacific coconuts show clear signs of domestication, such as a dwarf habit, self-pollination and rounded fruits. Indo-Atlantic coconuts keep the ancestral traits of tall growth and elongated triangular fruits.

science.text: Tattooing in Oceania was done with hand-tapping methods that have stayed largely unchanged for over 2,000 years. Comb-type tattoo chisels found in Polynesia closely resemble bone instruments from Arku Cave in northern Luzon, dated to before 1500 BCE.
Edward Winslow Gifford used the recently invented carbon dating on charcoal from his excavations in the 1950s. It dated the artifacts to between 2,800 and 2,450 years bp.

Papuans and Melanesians tattooed with distinctive obsidian skin piercers. Some sites with these tools date to around 1650 to 2000 BCE, older than the Austronesian expansion, suggesting a tattooing tradition already existed in the region.

culture.text: In the mid-2nd millennium BC, a distinctive culture called Lapita appeared suddenly in the Bismarck Archipelago of north-west Melanesia. It stands out in the archaeological record for its large permanent villages on beach terraces along the coasts.

Between about 2000 and 1000 BC, speakers of Austronesian languages spread through Maritime South-East Asia, almost certainly starting out from Taiwan. They moved into the edges of western Micronesia and on into Melanesia, leaving well-defined archaeological traces that let researchers follow and date their path.

A 2022 genetic study found that Micronesia was settled by three separate streams of First Remote Oceanian lineage. The first settled the Mariana Islands around 2800 BCE, a second reached Palau around 2400 BCE, and a third arrived in Central Micronesia around 2100 BCE.
Pottery is particularly characteristic of Lapita culture. Its makers produced a great many vessels of varied shapes, and some were distinguished by fine patterns and motifs pressed into the clay.

Between about 1300 and 900 BC, within a mere three or four centuries, Lapita culture spread 6000 km east from the Bismarck Archipelago. It reached as far as Fiji, Samoa and Tonga, the region where distinctive Polynesian culture then developed.

Austronesian navigators from the eastern islands of Indonesia made their way to New Guinea and Melanesia from 1500 BC onwards, then on to the islands of distant Oceania. Tonga, in western Polynesia, was first settled around 3,300 years ago.

The Lapita culture appeared suddenly in the Bismarck Archipelago in the mid-2nd millennium BC. It is known for large permanent villages on beach terraces and for pottery, including many vessels of varied shapes, some with fine patterns pressed into the clay.
In the region where Polynesian culture developed, Melanesian men would marry into the Lapita culture. Polynesians would then not move further east for another 1,000 years.

The 2022 study found that the peoples of Central Micronesia and Palau have a degree of Papuan ancestry. This ancestry is absent from the peoples of the Mariana Islands, who were the first of the three settlement streams.

Samoans have long held that their people were birthed from a tear in the heavens. Linguists and anthropologists theorize instead that migrants from Maritime Southeast Asia, travelling via Island Melanesia, reached the Samoan Islands approximately 3500 years ago.

The 2022 genetic study also supports the Admiralty Islands as the source of the Central Micronesian peoples and languages. The Admiralty Islands lie about 240 km north of the Bismarck Archipelago, which was settled by Oceanians thousands of years earlier.

Tonga, in western Polynesia, was first settled around 3,300 years ago. The Austronesian navigators who got there had made their way from the eastern islands of Indonesia, reaching New Guinea and Melanesia from 1500 BC onwards.
